style_when: scale is the story — a port, a refinery, a data centre hall, a rail yard, a skyline of cranes — and the reader needs to feel how big it is
prompt: A 200mm telephoto compression photograph down a data center hot aisle, a bright oxidised-red steel deny gate closed across the left rack row, its safety-yellow latch catching a single overhead cool-white light from the right, while a parallel open rack row on the right recedes toward a dark blue vanishing point. Charcoal rack cabinets with cobalt status LEDs, galvanised steel floor, compressed perspective, crystal-clear telephoto clarity, one-point perspective with gate off-center left. No people, no text, no logos.
rationale: The story is systemic software infrastructure and enforcement at scale; a compressed telephoto industrial shot of a data hall makes the deny path physical and legible without reducing the story to a single product or document.
cue: a release gate needs a deny path
subject: a bright red physical deny gate closed across a data-center rack row, with an adjacent open rack row in the same hallway
core_thesis: The intervention that changes an agent's error rate is the one that withholds the failed effect rather than merely warning about it; a release gate needs a deny path and permission to answer "cannot be determined" before it needs a better judge.
core_conflict: Detection already works, but enforcement does not: models acknowledge warnings and still print the faulty value, so a denial mechanism is the only thing that changes outcomes.
composition: compressed telephoto one-point perspective down the aisle, gate off-center left third blocking forward motion, rack rows receding to a vanishing point
